findings.headline: Pricing page offers a free start. It shows only paid plans.
findings.explanation: No trial length, no card policy, and no explanation of what activation changes.

claim_a.quote: Kick the tires for free and only upgrade when you're ready to activate.

findings.why_not_just_wording: One sentence offers a free route in and the rest of the page documents only paid ones.
findings.caveat: The answer is likely in the FAQ, which is collapsed and did not render for us. The comparison table rendered without values for the same reason.

findings.headline: Terms allow price changes at any time, with no notice period.
findings.explanation: Together these let a renewing price move without warning. Nothing on the pricing page sets an expectation either way.

claim_a.quote: We may change prices at any time.

claim_b.quote: Subscriptions will automatically renew for the same subscription period unless you cancel the account by the end of the then-current subscription period.

findings.why_not_just_wording: The two clauses combine into a commercial term that appears nowhere the buyer decides.
findings.caveat: Ordinary boilerplate in the right place, and your 30-day money back guarantee already gives customers a way out.

coverage_notes.what_was_not_checkable: This is the weakest coverage of the ten companies and we would rather say so than pad the report. The plan comparison on your pricing page rendered as a list of feature names with no per-plan values, so we could not check a single feature entitlement against your documentation. The FAQ rendered as a heading with no questions or answers. Your help site returned almost no readable text. We could not check the two things most worth checking here: which features are Basic versus Premium, and what your free entry route actually is. Your 30-day money back guarantee and your refund clause do agree with each other, which is worth saying, because that is the pair that most often does not.
